subsection: 9. The impact of war on society and economy; case study: women in the workforce during World War I

notes.h: Total war and the mobilisation of society
notes.b: The scale of the war meant that governments controlled industry, labour, food and propaganda, and the civilian population was drawn into the war effort.
points: Total war required governments to direct the economy, control prices and wages, and mobilise civilians as well as soldiers.
Britain's Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), passed in August 1914, gave the government wide powers over property, labour, the press and public behaviour.
The government took control of the railways in Britain in December 1916 and of the coal mines in 1917, to coordinate supplies for war.
Propaganda was used to recruit soldiers, sell war bonds and encourage civilians to accept shortages and sacrifice.
War loans and taxation increased the national debt of the belligerent states, and inflation reduced the real value of wages and savings.
Food shortages and rationing grew in Germany, where the harvest failures of 1916 led to the winter known as the Turnip Winter of 1916 to 1917.
The influenza pandemic of 1918 killed many people already weakened by war and food shortages; it is estimated to have killed tens of millions worldwide.

notes.b: Before the war most women who worked for pay were unmarried and worked in low-paid jobs, and the war opened up a wider range of employment to them.
points: Domestic service was the largest single employer of women in Britain before 1914, and it was poorly paid and offered few rights.
Women worked in the textile industries, in clothing and in small workshops, and they were usually paid well below men for similar work.
Married women rarely worked outside the home in Britain, France and Germany before the war, and women who did were generally from poorer families.
Trade unions were largely male-dominated, and many skilled unions excluded women from membership or refused to admit them to skilled trades.

notes.h: Case study: women in munitions and industry
points: Britain's Ministry of Munitions, created in 1915 under Lloyd George, employed large numbers of women in munitions factories, and by 1918 women made up a large share of the munitions workforce.
The Munitions of War Act of July 1915 made it illegal for workers in munitions to leave their jobs without permission, and it allowed women to replace men in skilled work.
Munitionettes, as the women workers were known, filled shells and made cordite, and many worked long shifts in dangerous conditions.
Working with TNT turned skin yellow and damaged health, which earned the women the nickname canary girls.
In France the munitions factories, including the Renault works at Billancourt, employed large numbers of women, and the French government encouraged women to replace men in industry.

In Germany the Auxiliary Service Law of December 1916 required men aged 17 to 60 to register for war service, and women were increasingly drawn into munitions work, though they were not conscripted in the same way as men.
Women in the transport sector worked as tram conductors, railway porters and drivers, and in Britain women drove ambulances and lorries during the war.

notes.h: Case study: women in offices, farms and services
points: Women replaced men in clerical work in Britain, France and Germany, and the number of women office workers rose sharply during the war.
The Women's Land Army was formed in Britain in 1917 to replace men on farms, and women worked as ploughmen, dairy workers and labourers.
The Voluntary Aid Detachments (VADs), formed in 1909, provided nursing and auxiliary services in hospitals, and during the war their numbers grew rapidly.
Edith Cavell, a British nurse who ran a training school in Brussels, was executed by the Germans in October 1915 for helping Allied soldiers escape occupied Belgium.
The Women's Royal Naval Service (WRNS) and the Women's Auxiliary Army Corps (WAAC), formed in 1917, employed women as cooks, clerks, drivers and telephonists in support of the armed forces.
The Women's Royal Air Force was formed in April 1918, and it employed women in mechanical and administrative roles.

notes.h: Case study: pay, unions and Pankhurst's campaigning
points: Women's wages for war work were usually lower than men's, and employers used women to dilute skilled work and reduce labour costs.

The Treasury Agreement of March 1915 between the government and the trade unions allowed women to be employed on men's work temporarily, on the condition that the work would return to men after the war.
Male trade unionists often resented women taking skilled work and feared that women would be used to undercut male pay, which caused tension in factories.

Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughter Christabel suspended the militant campaign of the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU) in August 1914 and campaigned for women's right to serve the war effort.
Emmeline Pankhurst formed the Women's Party in 1917, which campaigned for women's rights and for the social reforms that the war had made possible.
The war gave women greater public visibility, and many contemporaries saw their war work as proof of women's capacity to vote and take on public responsibilities.
The Representation of the People Act of February 1918 gave the vote in Britain to men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification.
Women gained full equality in the franchise in Britain in 1928, when the voting age for women was lowered to 21.
In Germany a decree of 12 November 1918 gave women the vote and the right to stand for election, and women were elected to the National Assembly in January 1919.
France did not give women the vote until 1944, despite women's large contribution to the war economy.
After the war many women lost their jobs as men returned, and governments and employers encouraged women to return to domestic life, although many women kept office and service jobs.

notes.h: Assessment: did the war change women's position?
notes.b: Historians differ on whether the war was a turning point for women or a temporary expansion of their role that was reversed after 1918.
points: Achievement: women's wartime work increased their economic independence and their public presence, and it contributed to the extension of the vote in Britain and Germany.
Limit: most women were pushed out of skilled war work after 1918, and the wartime gains in employment and wages were not sustained.
Achievement: the trade unions and government accepted women in many industrial and clerical roles that had been closed to them before 1914.
Limit: women still faced lower pay and discrimination after the war, and the franchise gains were limited by age and property qualifications.
Some historians argue that the war had only a limited effect because the postwar return to normality was strong, while others see it as a decisive step towards modern women's roles.

keyTerms.definition: A war in which whole societies and economies are mobilised, so that governments control industry, labour, food and propaganda.
The compulsory enlistment of men into the armed forces, which Britain introduced in 1916 and which shaped the labour market by taking men away from industry.
A war fought across several continents by a large number of states, in which the civilian population as well as the armed forces was drawn into the war effort.
The women who made shells, cordite and other munitions in British factories during the First World War.
The replacement of skilled male workers by unskilled or semi-skilled workers, including women, on tasks that had previously required skill.
The British wartime law of August 1914 that gave the government wide powers over labour, property, the press and public behaviour.
